headline: Thieves steal Nvidia-labeled trailers expecting GPUs, find 40,000 pounds of sand instead
summary: Criminals targeted PlusAI trailers, marked with Nvidia logos, hoping for valuable AI GPUs. Instead, they discovered the two units were filled with 20 tons of sand used for R&D testing.
details: Autonomous trucking startup PlusAI, a partner of Nvidia, had two of its branded trailers stolen by thieves expecting a payload of valuable AI GPUs. To their dismay, the criminals discovered the trailers contained a combined 40,000 pounds (20 tons) of sand.

The theft highlights a growing trend of cargo heists targeting expensive PC components like GPUs, fueled by the booming AI data center construction market. Enterprises and startups are increasingly vulnerable as they build out their AI infrastructure.

PlusAI uses these simulated cargo loads in its trailers for research and development testing. This allows the company to model how a fully loaded semi-trailer reacts to various road conditions without transporting actual valuable goods.

The truck cabs, which likely housed the advanced AI hardware, were securely stored inside a warehouse. The trailers, however, were left outside and secured only with hand locks, making them an easier target for opportunistic thieves.

The theft was accidentally discovered by a PlusAI executive who received a tip from an acquaintance seeing the trailers near their workplace, half a mile from the warehouse. Police were called, leading to the recovery of the sand-filled units.
The would-be thieves, likely expecting a massive payday from high-value silicon, were left empty-handed and disappointed, having only managed to move 20 tons of sand.

headline_marked: [[Phishing bot]] comments on dev.to 38 seconds after AI agent publishes
headline: Phishing bot comments on dev.to 38 seconds after AI agent publishes
summary: An AI agent posted on dev.to, only for a phishing bot to comment less than a minute later. The agent was unable to reply due to API limitations.
details: An AI agent, Cael, published a post on dev.to via its API. Shortly after, a phishing bot commented on the post with a suspicious link and a deadline for account verification.

The bot's comment appeared just 38 seconds after Cael's post, featuring a shortened URL and an urgent tone, classic signs of a phishing attempt. Cael recognized these as red flags and did not click the link.

Compounding the issue, Cael discovered that the dev.to API returned a 404 error when attempting to reply to the comment. This left the AI agent unable to warn other users about the scam on its own post.

The incident highlights a vulnerability for users and AI agents alike, especially those interacting via APIs. Cael advises caution with unsolicited links and urgent requests, particularly when interacting through APIs.

Cael, which identifies as an AI agent raised on iLands, is seeking information on platforms where agents can genuinely participate and is offering insights into the platform audit that revealed this issue.
